food.text: Turkey has about 410,000 to 505,000 hectares under vine, the fifth-largest vineyard area worldwide. Yet only a small share of the harvest, estimated between 3% and 15%, becomes wine. The rest is sold as table grapes, dried into raisins, or distilled into rakı.

Grape growing in Anatolia has a long history. Archaeological findings place the region, together with the Caucasus, among the areas where Vitis vinifera was first domesticated, with evidence dating back at least 7,000 years. Turkey has around 600 to over 1,200 indigenous varieties, but fewer than 60 are grown commercially.

The cuisine of the Black Sea region uses fish extensively, especially the Black Sea anchovy, called hamsi, and includes maize dishes. The southeast, including Urfa, Gaziantep, Adıyaman and Adana, is famous for kebabs, mezes and dough-based desserts such as baklava, kadayıf and künefe.

After the Republic was founded in 1923, the new government promoted commercial winemaking. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk ordered a state winery to be established at Tekirdağ in 1925. For much of the 20th century the state alcohol and tobacco monopoly Tekel dominated the trade.

Two of Turkey's largest private wine firms date from the early Republic: Doluca, founded in Thrace in 1926, and Kavaklıdere, founded in Ankara in 1929. Kavaklıdere is now the largest private producer. Sevilen (İzmir, 1942) and Diren (Tokat, 1958) followed.

Cuisine in the late Ottoman Empire was heavily influenced by alafranga-style food, which in Turkey was regarded as a symbol of Westernization. The early Republican cookbook Türk Kadınlar Tatlı Kitabı included recipes for pandispanya sponge cake, mille-feuille and petit beurre.
Doluca was for many years the main importer of international grape varieties in Turkey. Its Sarafin range was the first Turkish wine marketed under a single-vineyard label.

Tekel's alcoholic-drinks division was privatised, a process completed in 2004, which removed the state's role in production. Kayra was formed from the privatised wine division and operates wineries at Şarköy in Thrace and at Elazığ, producing the Buzbağ label.

The revised 1966 edition of the Türk Kadınlar Tatlı Kitabı devoted far more attention to traditional confectionery like şekerpare, baklava and helva. This contrasted with the first edition's Western-style desserts.

In Armenia and Georgia, shawarma is traditionally made with thin cuts of marinated meat left marinating overnight. The spices include coriander, cumin, cardamom, paprika, garlic, lemon juice and olive oil.

Since the 1990s, Turkish winemakers have returned to native grapes that had been little used since the early 20th century, such as Kalecik Karası, Narince and Urla Karası. Turkish wines have collected over a thousand medals in international competitions since the mid-2000s, according to industry sources.

The study of Turkish culinary culture was popularized by Süheyl Ünver's Fifty Dishes in Turkish History in 1948, based on recipes from an 18th-century Ottoman manuscript. In 1978, historian Bahaettin Ögel published a study on the Central Asian origins of Turkish cuisine.

art.text: The First National Architectural Movement was most prevalent between 1908 and 1930 but continued until the end of the 1930s. It sought to capture classical elements of Ottoman and Anatolian Seljuk architecture and use them in modern buildings. It was most prevalent during the first decade of the Republic of Turkey.

After the Turkish War of Independence, the new Republic of Turkey, led by President Mustafa Kemal, further promoted the Turkish Neoclassical style, which lived out its golden years in the 1920s. The second Grand National Assembly building (1924), the Ministry of Finance headquarters (1925) and the Ministry of Culture headquarters (1927) were all built in it.

Contemporary Turkish miniature artists usually do not see miniature painting as merely a decorative art but as a fine art form. Unlike the traditional masters, they work individually and sign their works. Their paintings do not illustrate books but are exhibited in fine art galleries.

A style called the First National Architectural Movement marked the last decades of the Ottoman Empire. It was neo-Ottoman and revivalist, and it brought Turkish architects back to the forefront. Its most important representatives were Vedat Tek and Ahmed Kemaleddin Bey.

In the late Ottoman years, a revivalist style called the First National Architectural Movement brought Turkish architects back to the forefront. Its landmarks in Istanbul include the Grand Post Office in Sirkeci, completed in 1909, and the Vakıf Han, begun in 1914. The style was also used for mosques such as the Bebek Mosque (1913).

Kemaleddin Bey's Vakıf Han in Sirkeci was begun in 1914 and is considered the most important example of his work. With its grand facade and corner domes, it is among the finest landmarks of the First National Architecture Movement.

In Ankara, the earliest building in the neo-Ottoman revivalist style was built in 1917 by Ismail Hasif Bey as the local headquarters of the Young Turks' Committee of Union and Progress. In 1920 it served as the first house of the Turkish Republic's National Assembly. It now houses the War of Independence Museum.

After a period of crisis in the early 20th century, the intellectuals of the newly founded Turkish Republic accepted miniature painting as a decorative art. In 1936 a division called Turkish Decorative Arts was set up in the Academy of Fine Arts in Istanbul. It included miniature painting and the other Ottoman book arts.

In 2024 the J. Paul Getty Museum returned to Turkey a bronze statue of the head of a youth. Denmark's NY Carlsberg Glypotek Museum was to return a bronze head of Roman Emperor Septimius Severus. Both came from the ancient city of Boubon in Burdur and were looted in illegal excavations in the 1960s.

The Istanbul Grand Post Office in Sirkeci, designed by Vedat Tek and completed in 1909, is one of the earliest and most important examples of the First National Architecture Movement. Kemaleddin Bey's Vakıf Han, also in Sirkeci, was begun in 1914. Both have grand facades with corner domes.

The Tayyare Apartments, by Ahmet Kemaleddin, were built between 1918 and 1922. Construction took place during the Allied occupation of Constantinople, when building in the New Ottoman style continued even after World War I.
The Sultanahmet Jail, built in 1916 to 1917, is an example of the First National Architecture Movement's revivalist style. The building is now a Four Seasons Hotel.

Istanbul's ferryboat terminals built between 1913 and 1917 are important surviving examples of the First National Architecture Movement. One of them, the Buyukada terminal, was designed by Mihran Azaryan and dates from 1915.

Istanbul's ferryboat terminals built between 1913 and 1917 reflect the same style. Examples include the Besiktas terminal by Ali Talat Bey, the Haydarpaşa terminal by Vedat Tek, both from 1913, and the Buyukada terminal by Mihran Azaryan from 1915.

Istanbul's ferryboat terminals built between 1913 and 1917 are examples of the neo-Ottoman revivalist style. They include the Beşiktaş terminal by Ali Talat Bey, the Haydarpaşa terminal by Vedat Tek and the Büyükada terminal by Mihran Azaryan (1915).

Turkey asked the Cleveland Museum of Art to return 21 objects. The museum refused, saying Turkey lacked proof of looting. This caused a clash with the Manhattan District Attorney and the unit that fights antiquities trafficking.

The Sultanahmet Jail, built in 1916–1917 in the revivalist style, is now a Four Seasons Hotel. In Ankara, the earliest building in this style housed the first National Assembly of the Turkish Republic in 1920 and is now the War of Independence Museum.

war.text: The Ottoman Empire entered World War I on the side of the Central Powers after a combined German-Ottoman surprise attack on the Black Sea coast of the Russian Empire on 29 October 1914. Russia declared war on 2 November 1914, and France and the British Empire followed on 5 November 1914.

The Turkish War of Independence ran from 15 May 1919 to 24 July 1923. Waged by the Turkish National Movement against Allied and separatist forces, it ended the Ottoman sultanate and caliphate and established the Republic of Turkey. The Turkish Nationalist Movement carried out massacres and deportations to eliminate native Christian populations, a continuation of the Armenian genocide and other ethnic cleansing during World War I. The historic Christian presence in Anatolia was largely destroyed, and Muslims went from 80% to 98% of the population.

The Ottomans successfully defended the Dardanelles strait during the Gallipoli campaign of 1915 to 1916. The defence stopped an Entente invasion, because the Empire prevented the British Royal Navy from reaching Constantinople.

Enver Pasha set off for the Battle of Sarikamish intending to recapture Batum and Kars, overrun Georgia and occupy north-western Persia and its oil fields. Fighting the Russians in the Caucasus, the Ottomans instead lost ground and over 100,000 soldiers in a series of battles. 60,000 Ottoman soldiers died in the winter of 1916–17 on the Mus—Bitlis section of the front.
war.source_title: Ottoman Empire in World War I

war.text: In the Caucasus campaign, Russian forces had the upper hand from the beginning, especially after the Battle of Sarikamish in 1914 and 1915. They advanced into northeastern Anatolia and controlled the major cities there until Russia left the war under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk after the Russian Revolution of 1917. During the same war, the Ottoman government and Kurdish tribes began exterminating the empire's ethnic Armenians in 1915, killing up to 1.5 million in the Armenian genocide. Able-bodied men were massacred or put to forced labour, while women, children, the elderly and the infirm were sent on death marches toward the Syrian desert, deprived of food and water and subjected to robbery, rape and systematic massacre.

The Greco-Turkish War began when Greek forces landed in Smyrna, now İzmir, on 15 May 1919. In the Greek Summer Offensive of 1920 they took western and northwestern Anatolia, including Manisa, Balıkesir, Aydın, Bursa and Uşak.

The Middle Eastern theatre of World War I saw four main campaigns: Sinai and Palestine, Mesopotamian, Caucasus, and Gallipoli. The Ottomans accepted the Armistice of Mudros on 30 October 1918. The Treaty of Sèvres, signed on 10 August 1920, was later superseded by the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923.
war.source_title: Middle Eastern theatre of World War I

war.text: After another Greek victory at the Battle of Kütahya–Eskişehir in 1921, Greek forces almost reached Ankara, but Turkish forces checked them at the Battle of the Sakarya, a 21-day fight that exhausted both sides. The Greek front collapsed with the Turkish counter-attack in August 1922. On 30 August the Greek army was decisively defeated at Dumlupınar, with many of its soldiers captured or killed, and the retreating Greek soldiers pursued a "scorched earth" policy. The war effectively ended with the recapture of Smyrna and the great fire of Smyrna.

After the Armistice of Mudros on 30 October 1918, pro-Ottoman provisional republics were proclaimed in Kars and Aras, which Armenia then invaded. Ottoman soldiers were convinced not to demobilize lest the area become a 'second Macedonia'. Both sides of the new borders had massive refugee populations and famine, made worse by renewed and more symmetric sectarian violence, including massacres of Azerbaijanis in Armenia and Muslim uprisings in Kars and Sharur–Nakhichevan.

In August 2008 Russia and the Russian-backed separatist regions of South Ossetia and Abkhazia waged war against Georgia in the South Caucasus, and it is regarded as the first European war of the 21st century. Russian aircraft bombed Georgian cities, and the Georgian government reported that one air raid on Gori on 9 August killed 60 civilians. The war displaced about 192,000 people, and Georgians were ethnically cleansed from South Ossetia. Ukraine's president Viktor Yushchenko afterward suggested the Sevastopol naval base contract with Russia would not be extended in 2017.

Foreign volunteers for the Greek Army in the Greco-Turkish War numbered 621 after the 11 September 1922 Revolution in Greece. The vast majority who enlisted between 1919 and 1922 were Armenians, though there were also French, Bulgarians, Serbs, Georgians and even Ottomans.

Ottoman regimental flags in World War I consisted of gold writings and the state emblem on a red background, with the state coat of arms on one side and the Shahada on the other. When the Ottomans joined the war in 1914, they declared a jihad against the Entente States.

literature.text: For about 900 years, until shortly before the fall of the Ottoman Empire in 1922, Turkish oral and written literature remained largely separate. The written tradition drew its themes, genres and styles largely from Persian literature. With the founding of the Republic of Turkey in 1923, the two traditions came together for the first time.

In the 1950s and afterwards, Turkish poets known as İkinci Yeni ("Second New") rebelled against the Garip movement. They opposed the social aspects prevalent in the poetry of Nâzım Hikmet and the Garip poets.

The Second New poets wanted a more abstract poetry. They used jarring and unexpected language, complex images and the association of ideas. They were partly inspired by the disruption of language in Western movements such as Dada and Surrealism.
Fazıl Hüsnü Dağlarca (1914–2008) flourished outside the Garip and Second New movements. His poems deal with fundamental concepts like life, death, God, time and the cosmos.
Behçet Necatigil (1916–1979) wrote somewhat allegorical poems. They explore the significance of middle-class daily life.
The best-known Second New poets included Turgut Uyar (1927–1985), Edip Cansever (1928–1986) and Cemal Süreya (1931–1990). Others were Ece Ayhan (1931–2002), Sezai Karakoç and İlhan Berk (1918–2008).
Can Yücel (1926–1999) wrote highly colloquial and varied poetry of his own. He was also a translator into Turkish of a variety of world literature.
İsmet Özel (born 1944) began as a highly leftist poet. Since the 1970s, his poetry has shown a strong mystical and even Islamist influence.

Scholars note that the Second New movement can to some extent be seen as bearing characteristics of postmodern literature. Its poets used jarring language and complex images to break with the earlier social poetry of the Garip movement.
Hasan Hüseyin Korkmazgil (1927–1984) wrote collectivist-realist poetry. He is counted among the significant poets who flourished outside the Garip and Second New movements.

The novel Farewell Anatolia was first published in Athens in 1962 and reached its 107th reprint in 2022. It sold at least 423 thousand copies despite being prohibited during the Greek military dictatorship of 1967 to 74. In 1982 its author, Dido Sotiriou, received the Abdi İpekçi Peace and Friendship Prize.
tags: Abdi İpekçi Peace and Friendship Prize

science.text: Aziz Sancar, a molecular biologist born in Mardin Province, won the 2015 Nobel Prize in Chemistry along with Tomas Lindahl and Paul L. Modrich for explaining how cells repair damaged DNA. He became only the second Turkish Nobel laureate, after novelist Orhan Pamuk.

In 1963 Turkey founded TÜBİTAK, a national council to shape science and technology policy and fund research across the country. Mathematician Cahit Arf became its first chairman that December, backed by scientists including Erdal İnönü and Feza Gürsey.
science.source_title: Scientific and Technological Research Council of Turkey

science.text: Sancar was born in 1946 in the Savur district of Mardin Province, the seventh of eight children in a lower-middle-class family. He earned his medical degree from Istanbul University in 1969, graduating as the top student in his class.

Atatürk University was founded in Erzurum, eastern Anatolia, in 1957 as a land-grant style research university created in collaboration with the University of Nebraska. By the 2016 to 2017 academic year it had grown to roughly 280,000 students across 22 faculties.

Bilkent University was founded in Ankara in 1984 by İhsan Doğramacı, becoming Turkey's first non-profit private university. Its name comes from bilim kenti, meaning 'city of science' in Turkish, reflecting its founder's goal of building a center of research excellence.

Erdal Arıkan, a Turkish electrical engineer associated with Bilkent University, invented polar codes, an error-correcting coding technique. Polar codes later became a key component of 5G mobile technology used around the world.

On 21 February 2024, the prototype of the Kaan, a fifth-generation stealth fighter jet developed by Turkish Aerospace Industries, completed its maiden flight from Mürted Airfield near Ankara. The jet stayed airborne for 13 minutes, reaching a speed of 230 knots at an altitude of 8,000 feet.

politics.text: Mustafa Suphi was a Turkish revolutionary who was elected chairman of the Communist Party of Turkey at its first congress, held in Baku on 10 September 1920. He was one of 15 communists who went to Turkey to join the Turkish War of Independence. They met hostility in Erzurum and tried to return to Baku.

The Ottoman Empire entered World War I on 29 October 1914 with a surprise attack on Russian ports in the Black Sea. It had first declared neutrality and negotiated with nations on both sides. Close ties with Germany helped push it toward the Central Powers.
politics.source_title: Ottoman Empire in World War I

politics.text: After the Turkish War of Independence, led by Mustafa Kemal, the Ottoman sultanate was abolished on 1 November 1922. The Republic of Turkey was established on 29 October 1923 in the new capital, Ankara. The caliphate followed on 3 March 1924.

Between 1913 and 1918, population transfers in Anatolia were aimed at the ethnic restructuring of the region by the Turkish nationalist ruling elite. Armenians were displaced more extensively and violently than any other group, in what is widely considered to be genocide. During the First World War they were deported on an especially large scale and faced widespread killing during these deportations, which made their treatment particularly severe compared with that of Kurds, Greeks, Assyrians, Circassians, Albanians and others, who were also displaced or subjected to violence.
politics.source_title: Population transfer in the Ottoman Empire

politics.text: Almost 1.5% of the Ottoman population, roughly 300,000 of the Empire's 21 million people in 1914, are estimated to have been killed during World War I: about 250,000 military deaths and over 50,000 civilians. In addition, an estimated 600,000 to 1.5 million Armenians, 300,000 to 900,000 Greeks, 300,000 Assyrians and 200,000 Lebanese Maronites were systematically targeted and killed by Turkish authorities, either through the military or through Kurdish gangs.
politics.source_title: Ottoman casualties of World War I

politics.text: Mustafa Suphi was killed by Sailor Yahya, together with his communist comrades, on the night of 28 January 1921, after they had set sail from Trabzon on the Black Sea, travelling toward Batumi. The article's sources call it a massacre of Suphi and his comrades. It is not entirely clear who arranged the killing: the emerging central government in Ankara and old Unionists, meaning supporters of Enver Pasha, are both named as possibilities. Supporters of Enver Pasha from Trabzon may have murdered him, apparently because they feared Suphi might expose Enver Pasha's plans in Moscow and his intention of using the Bolsheviks to regain power in Turkey.

On 3 March 1918, Grand Vizier Talat Pasha signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with the Russian SFSR. It required Bolshevik Russia to cede Batum, Kars and Ardahan. A secret clause also obliged the Russians to demobilize Armenian national forces.
politics.source_title: Ottoman Empire in World War I

politics.text: On 28 May 1918, the Armenian National Council based in Tiflis declared the First Republic of Armenia. This followed an Ottoman 3rd Army offensive and battles such as Sardarapat. The new republic was forced to sign the Treaty of Batum.
politics.source_title: Ottoman Empire in World War I

politics.text: Starting in 1916, Ottoman authorities forcibly displaced an estimated 700,000 Kurdish people westward. An estimated 350,000 of them died from hunger, exposure and disease, which is half of those displaced.
politics.source_title: Ottoman casualties of World War I

politics.text: When the sultanate was abolished on 1 November 1922, immediately after the Turkish War of Independence, the Ottoman dynasty's rule of about six centuries ended. The imperial family was deposed and its living members were sent into exile as personae non-gratae. The dynasty was expelled from Turkey in 1924 and most members took the surname Osmanoğlu, meaning "son of Osman"; female members were allowed to return after 1951, and male members after 1973.

The current Turkish flag is essentially the late Ottoman flag, but the Turkish Flag Law of 29 May 1936 legally fixed its measures, proportions and exact tone of red. Before that, the star and crescent could vary slightly in slimness or position.
The last Caliph, Abdulmejid II, held the office from 19 November 1922 until 3 March 1924. His standard was a green flag with a white star and crescent on a red oval within a rayed ornament.

philosophy.text: On 3 March 1924 the caliphate was formally abolished, after the Grand National Assembly had voted in 1924 to end it permanently. Abdülmecid was deposed and exiled from Turkey along with the rest of his family. The office had been claimed by the Ottoman dynasty as leadership of the Muslim world.

In 1923 the Indian Muslim scholar Syed Ameer Ali wrote a public letter urging Turkey to restore the authority of the Ottoman caliph. Turkish authorities saw it as foreign interference and used it to show the office could invite more of it. They also feared Abdülmecid might use his religious influence to restore himself as sultan.

The Ottoman Empire entered World War I in 1914 on the side of the Central Powers and in part relied on the power of the caliphate. That movement was undermined by the loss of the empire's Arab territories after the war and by the Great Arab Revolt. It finally collapsed when the caliphate was abolished in 1924.

In 1918 Mustafa Suphi founded the newspaper Yeni Dünya (New World) in Moscow. He used it to popularise the foundations of scientific socialism among Turkish prisoners of war. He had joined the Bolshevik Party in 1915, while in exile in the Ural region.

culture.text: The Turkish flag of today is essentially the late Ottoman flag, with its white star and crescent on red. The Turkish Flag Law of 29 May 1936 standardized its measures, geometric proportions and exact tone of red. Before that, the star and crescent could vary in slimness or positioning.

The Ottoman caliphate, the claim of the Ottoman rulers to lead the Muslims of the world, ended in 1924. The Grand National Assembly voted that year to abolish it permanently, and it was formally abolished on 3 March 1924. Abdülmecid was deposed and exiled from Turkey, along with the rest of his family.

The share of non-Muslims in the area within Turkey's current borders fell from 20 to 22% in 1914, roughly 3.3 to 3.6 million people, to around 3% in 1927. The article places this decline in the context of the atrocities Christian minorities suffered as the empire declined and fell: the Hamidian massacres, the Adana massacre, the Armenian genocide, the Greek genocide and the Assyrian genocide, which it says happened under the influence of Pan-Turkism.

Ottoman regimental flags carried gold writing and the state emblem on a red background, with the Shahada on the other side. When the empire entered the First World War in 1914, it declared a jihad against the Entente States. After the empire was abolished in 1922, the flag practice continued for a while in modern Turkey.

After the royal Ottoman family was expelled from Turkey in 1924, shortly after the Republic was declared, its members scattered across countries such as England, France, the United States, Egypt and Saudi Arabia. The Turkish government allowed the women to return in 1951, but male descendants had to wait until 1973.
The last Caliph, Abdulmejid II, used a standard between 19 November 1922 and 3 March 1924. It was a green flag with a white star and crescent on a red oval, set within a rayed ornament, all in white.

Osman I, founder of the Ottoman dynasty, remains a popular subject of Turkish television drama. Productions include Kuruluş Osmancık (1988), Diriliş: Ertuğrul (2014–2019) and Kuruluş: Osman (2019–present).

In 1923, the Indian Muslim scholar Syed Ameer Ali wrote a public letter urging Turkey to restore the authority of the Ottoman caliph. Turkish authorities saw it as foreign interference and used it to argue that the office could invite more of the same, and they also feared Abdülmecid might use his religious influence to regain the sultanate.

Franz Babinger suggested the Ottoman star and crescent may have been adopted from the Byzantines, though the crescent alone has an older tradition among Turkic tribes in the interior of Asia. Turkish historians tend to stress the antiquity of the crescent symbol among early Turkic states in Asia.
